analysis.one_liner: Replaces the head of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau with a five-member commission.
analysis.headline: The House Financial Services Committee reported the bill 31–21 in February 2014, but it never received a House floor vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would replace the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's single Director with a five-member commission, including the Federal Reserve's Vice Chairman for Supervision and four presidential appointees confirmed by the Senate, with no more than two members from one political party. It would also bar the Commission Chair from submitting funding requests without the full Commission's approval. Because any member could be removed by the President at will and the bureau could operate before confirmations with a one-member quorum, the change would make the consumer regulator slower and more politically pliable, which is why banks and lenders favored it.
analysis.who_benefits: Banks, lenders, debt collectors and other financial companies overseen by the CFPB would benefit. A commission with staggered terms, vacancy rules, a one-member quorum before any Senate confirmations, at-will presidential removal, and a bar on the Chair submitting budget requests alone would slow rulemaking and enforcement and make outcomes easier to influence. Consumer advocates who supported the single-Director structure would lose the strong, independent enforcer they had.

how_it_helps.text: Replaces the single CFPB Director with a five-member Commission, no more than two of whom may belong to one political party, diluting the power of one official to direct consumer enforcement [S3].
Lets the President remove any Commissioner at will, unlike the current Director who can only be removed for cause, making the bureau more politically responsive to whoever holds the White House [S4].

Before even two members are confirmed, a single member would constitute a quorum to conduct bureau business, and the Chair could not submit funding requests without the Commission's approval, adding friction to the bureau's operations [S4].

analysis.who_pays: Consumers would bear the cost: slower rulemaking and weaker, less consistent enforcement against predatory lending, credit-reporting errors, and abusive debt collection, during vacancies and whenever the commission deadlocked along its party limits.

drawbacks.text: The strongest good-faith objection to the status quo it targets: one unelected Director now holds sweeping power over rules and enforcement, and other financial regulators like the SEC and FTC use commissions, which supporters argued would add balance and accountability [S3].

The bill's design undercuts that stated goal: at-will removal, a one-member quorum before confirmations, and five-year staggered terms mean long stretches where a single appointee or a deadlocked commission runs the bureau, slowing or stalling consumer protection [S4].

Requiring the full Commission's approval for budget requests would add a procedural choke point over a bureau that currently operates independently, the kind of friction that mostly benefits regulated firms seeking delay [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated rationale — replacing a powerful single Director with a bipartisan commission, as at the SEC and FTC — has some genuine appeal. But the specific design points away from accountability and toward paralysis and political control: the President could remove commissioners at will, the bureau could act through a single member before any confirmations, and the Chair's funding requests would need commission sign-off. The practical effect is slower, weaker consumer enforcement, which is what the regulated industry stood to gain; the cost falls on consumers the bureau was created to protect.

outcome.mechanism: The Financial Services Committee approved it 31–21 and reported it in February 2014, but House leadership never scheduled a floor vote and it sat on the Union Calendar until Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Rep. Spencer Bachus introduced the bill on June 20, 2013, and it was referred to the House Financial Services Committee [S1].
The committee marked it up on November 21, 2013, and ordered it reported as amended by a 31–21 vote [S6].
On February 6, 2014, the committee reported the bill with an amendment (H. Rept. 113-345) and it was placed on the Union Calendar, No. 255, meaning it was eligible for floor action [S3].
No floor vote ever occurred, and the bill died at the end of the 113th Congress on January 3, 2015 [S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers are better off that the bill died: the CFPB kept its single-Director structure and independent operation rather than shifting to a slower commission that banks and lenders had sought. The financial industry did not get the restructuring it wanted from this bill, though it pursued it in other vehicles.

for.name: Rep. Spencer Bachus
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to replace the CFPB Director with a five-member commission.

for.name: 15 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Democrats did.

for.name: House Financial Services Committee
for.what_they_did: Held a hearing and markup, then ordered the bill reported as amended by a 31–21 vote and reported it in February 2014.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled floor debate after the bill was placed on the Union Calendar in February 2014; it sat there until the Congress ended.

against.name: President Obama
against.what_they_did: The administration publicly opposed House Republican bills to restructure the CFPB, which had been created over industry objections by the 2010 Dodd-Frank law.

sides.party_line_note: All 15 cosponsors were Republicans, and the committee advanced it on a 31–21 vote; the bill moved only through a Republican-controlled committee and never reached the floor.

industries.industry: Banks, lenders, debt collectors and other financial firms overseen by the CFPB
industries.note: A commission with vacancy gaps, a party balance cap, and a chair stripped of independent funding-request authority would slow the rules and enforcement actions these firms face. Their gain is reduced oversight of the same practices that harm consumers.
Groups that built and defended the single-Director CFPB as a strong independent enforcer would lose the structure they fought for; the bill dismantles that structure without strengthening the bureau.
